A real-time support system for dysmenorrhea

View Prototype ↗ See the Solution
scroll
The problem

Menstrual pain is common, yet 79% of our respondents reported zero institutional support. The issue isn't the pain itself: it's the absence of support in places that demand uninterrupted productivity.

What I designed

Pause: a discreet, real-time support app for dysmenorrhea, anticipate & prep, one long-press Pain Mode for relief, and dignified assistance through Silent SOS and Privacy Mode.

My role

UX research, interaction design, UI and prototyping, plus evaluative testing, SUS, think-aloud and eye-tracking.

The result

SUS of 70.0 (Grade B). Eye-tracking showed 17.98s of fixation before relief, which exposed three friction points (UI-05, UI-01, UI-03) with redesigns shown below.

01

Onboarding & Profile Setup

Pause introduces itself gently. Users select their reasons for joining, rate pain severity, mark body areas, and choose an accessibility profile, mobility, sensory, or communication. A support circle is added, and cycle history is logged to seed predictions.

Accessibility ProfileSupport CircleCycle Baseline
02

7-Day Pre-Period Routine

Seven days before the predicted period, Pause surfaces a Pattern Insight card. It identifies correlations: high stress, low sleep, poor nutrition, and generates a personalised micro-plan. Users customise and confirm. Smart reminders fire at the right time.

Capacity HeatmapPattern InsightsAdaptive Plan
03

Pain Mode: Real-Time Relief

One long-press on the relief button activates Pain Mode. Cognitive load drops to zero. Users are immediately offered a Pause Kit nearby, a guided breathing session, audio relief, or an AI companion. A Pause Space can be found and booked directly from this screen.

Rapid Relief TriggerPause Kit LocatorAI Companion
04

Support Mode: Silent SOS

When users need human support, they select a contact, caregiver, manager, or trusted friend. An AI-drafted, stigma-neutral message is composed automatically. It can be edited, sent via WhatsApp, SMS, or email, and optionally includes a medical validation report.

Silent SOSPrivacy MaskingAI-Drafted Message
05

Clinical Hub & GA34 Passport

Users connect with verified menstrual health specialists for telehealth or in-person consultations. After consultation, a doctor-verified GA34 Clinical Passport is issued, a scannable badge that can be presented at college or workplace as official documentation for leave.

Telehealth PortalGA34 CertificationDysmenorrhea Badge

The Problem

The issue is not the pain itself:
it is the absence of support
in environments that demand
uninterrupted productivity.

70% of menstruators globally experience dysmenorrhea
80% of cases go untreated due to cultural normalisation
79% of our respondents reported zero institutional support
54% push through pain silently, out of fear of judgment
Research

Multi-layered
discovery

We conducted secondary literature review, a 78-person survey, 4 in-depth interviews (including disabled users), and a contextual enquiry on a college campus, building a full picture of lived experience.

01

Survey: 78 Respondents Globally

Distributed via Reddit and personal networks. Average pain score: 5.8/10. 44% scored 7 or above. 15% identified as having a disability. Privacy was the #1 requested feature (55%), followed by heat therapy (51%) and quiet spaces (49%).

02

4 Interviews: Diverse User Types

Tanya (deaf & mute, PCOD), Megha (severe pain 8–9/10), Mansi (banker, workplace context), Ananaya (mobility disability). All 4 hid their pain. All 4 defaulted to going home. None found public infrastructure adequate.

03

Contextual Enquiry: College Campus

Observed a student with temporary mobility impairment managing menstruation on campus. She continued attending despite visible distress, avoided movement, limited washroom use due to inaccessibility, and found no rest space.

04

Secondary Research: 8 Sources

Reviewed peer-reviewed journals (PMC6365059, PMC8943241, PMC9533282), government reports, and case studies. Found only 10% of 119 menstrual apps address pain directly. 25% get no relief from NSAIDs.

"Resting rooms could help, but it still comes with overthinking, how will the manager respond?"

Survey respondent, working professional

Key Insights

What the data
revealed

Pain is Invisible

All 4 interviewees hid their condition from peers & employers

Home is the Fallback

No public or campus space has ever served them during pain peaks

Infrastructure Fails

Dirty, inaccessible washrooms cited by all 4, no shelf, no bin, no dignity

Disability Compounds

The wheelchair user never found a single space meeting both needs simultaneously

Policy ≠ Protection

Mansi has 11 paid menstrual leaves and still faces stigma from managers

How Might We

The design
questions

How might we provide a person with severe dysmenorrhea with real-time, actionable support to manage pain episodes effectively?

How might we design discreet, stigma-free relief experiences within public and workplace environments?

How might we help users in high-pain distress make quick, intuitive decisions that provide "what to do now" guidance?

How might we create inclusive health solutions that support both temporary injuries and permanent disabilities?

The Solution

Meet Pause.

A discreet, real-time support app that helps individuals manage dysmenorrhea through actionable guidance, accessible interaction, and context-aware support, enabling them to navigate pain with autonomy and minimal disruption.

Beyond the screen

Relief that exists in the room, not only in the app.

Pain does not wait until you are somewhere comfortable. Two physical touchpoints extend the app into the places where support is missing, and each connects back to it.

Pause Space

A private recovery pod for a short break. Indirect warm lighting and acoustic panelling create calm and privacy, a control panel within easy reach sets heat, pulse, light, a breathing guide and a session timer, and targeted relief zones cover heat for the abdomen, pressure for the back and vibration for the thighs and legs.

Pause Kit

On-the-go menstrual relief in public washrooms. A wall-mounted kit offers pads, heat support, wipes and essentials, designed to be discreet, stigma-free and accessible for diverse needs. A QR code opens the Pause app for guidance, care tips and nearby support.

The emotional
vocabulary

"The Pause Journey, from Emotional Release to Recovery." A palette and typography system designed to feel like safety, not sterility.

Outcomes

What this
changes

By centering those most excluded, menstruators with pain, and those with disabilities, Pause creates ripple effects across dignity, productivity, and institutional culture.

5

Core Task Flows

Onboarding, 7-day prep, pain mode, support mode, and clinical hub, each designed for low-effort interaction during distress.

2-in-1

Physical + Digital

The Pause Space pod and the app work as a unified ecosystem, the first to address menstrual pain and disability needs simultaneously.

GA34

Clinical Validation

Users can generate ICD-11 certified documentation, shifting the proof burden away from the individual and toward institutional accountability.

Pain should not be the
price of showing up.

Pause is more than an app. It is a claim that menstrual pain is a design problem, one that public spaces, workplaces, and digital products have failed to solve. Until now.

Testing

When pain gets worse,
every extra decision matters.

I tested Pause under high-stress scenarios to understand where the interface helped, and where it made users work harder than necessary.

Evaluative Testing User Testing · Eye Tracking · SUS · Think-Aloud
01 / 05
01 · The moment

A fictionalized testing scenario

9/10Sarah's pain level, right now

Sarah is at work when the pain suddenly spikes.

She doesn't want to explain.
She doesn't want to search.
She just needs relief.

Can Pause help her get there?, Concept B, tested below.
02 · The friction

Relief kits were buried inside Pain Mode.

Cognitive Overload (Hick's Law)
Real eye-tracking heatmap of the Concept B Home screen (3 participants). Red is where attention concentrated.
17.98s Total fixation on Concept B's
insight card (3 participants)
Hick's Law
More choices
+ more processing
↓
slower decision-making

Under high pain, the interface was asking Sarah to make too many decisions before reaching relief.

A/B eye-tracking · 3 participants · 5 areas of interest

Two home screens, one question: where does attention land first?

Before testing the full flows, I compared two Home screen concepts on an eye-tracker. Concept A leads with a "Today's Highlight" AI insight; Concept B reframes it as a recovery-first "Prioritize Recovery" card with Quick Care shortcuts.

Total fixation by area (seconds)

Concept AConcept B
Insight card12.65s · 17.98s
Capacity heatmap15.71s · 8.69s
Quick actions5.64s · 5.61s
Navigation bar2.39s · 1.86s
Header0.00s · 0.00s

Totals combine all 3 participants.

What the gaze told us

  • The insight card won in both. It was the main entry point, and in Concept B it drew the most attention of any area (17.98s).
  • Concept B was found faster. Participants generally reached its main card sooner, but that did not always mean longer engagement.
  • Concept A encouraged exploring. More time on the heatmap and supporting content.
  • The header was ignored in both concepts, so the SOS and Relief icons placed there got no attention.
An honest caveat. None of the eye-tracking metrics reached statistical significance (all p > 0.05, n = 3). These are directional signals, so the final call was made on UX goals rather than on gaze data alone.

Industry average is 68. Pause's mean of 70.0 sits just above it; three of five participants scored above 68.

What moved the scores

Smart presets reduce effortPause Space booking auto-configures the room from the mood and pain just entered. P2 and P4 praised it.
Checkout and logging add frictionExtra taps in symptom logging (P1) and a heavy Pain Mode kit purchase flow (P3).
Onboarding feels long upfrontNine screens before Home delayed the "aha" moment (P2, P5).
Four fixes the SUS data pointed to
1
Simplify Pain Mode checkoutSaved kits and one-tap reorder, so relief takes 1 to 2 taps.
2
Shorten onboardingMove disability profile and support circle setup to an optional step after Home.
3
Consolidate plan customizationMerge three near-identical "Customize Your Plan" screens into one editable summary.
4
Extend the smart-preset patternApply Pause Space's mood-based auto-setup to Pain Mode and Support Mode.
04 · Where users got stuck

Think-Aloud Testing

UI-05
Hidden Relief Kits
Relief kits sat inside Pain Mode, several taps deep.
Finding
"It took me a while to find where the kit was." (P5). Three of five participants could not predict where Pause Kit lived, and "Pain Mode" itself confused them.
Global "Get Relief" FAB
A persistent floating action, visible from every screen, consistent with Pause's design system.
"Move the critical action to where the user needs it, not where the feature happens to live."
UI-01
Disappearing Routine Plan
The generated 7-day plan had no way to be reviewed after confirmation.
Finding
"The setup was easy, but I'm not sure where I'll see this plan again." (P5). Once generated, there was no persistent entry point back to it.
Persistent "My Plan" home tracker card
A live progress card pinned to Home, showing day-by-day status.
"Make important ongoing actions visible without forcing users to remember where they were."
UI-03
Low Contrast + Crop Issues
A dark header cropped its own content, and search was placed where it competed with primary actions.
Finding
Contrast between text and background made primary CTAs hard to locate, and search placement added friction to an already content-dense page.
WCAG AA contrast upgrade + search repositioning
Fixed-height header with full visibility, and search moved onto a clear surface.
"Accessibility isn't a final polish layer. It changes how information is perceived and found."
5 participants · 5 tasks · 11 usability issues

What I saw, and what I changed.

Every session was logged task by task: what people did, what they said and what I observed. Issues were merged across participants and ranked by severity.

IDIssueParticipantsSeverity
UI-05Pause Kit and SOS not anchored in the IA; "Pain Mode" naming confuses3/5High
UI-01No persistent "View Plan" entry; insight timing unclear2/5Medium
UI-03Weak CTA and text contrast on primary actions2/5Medium
UI-04Bottom nav behaves inconsistently on focused screens2/5Medium
UI-06Pause Space cards too dense for their size2/5Medium
UI-11Support Mode has one editable message template only2/5Medium
UI-07No way to view past consultations or leave feedback1/5Medium
UI-08Specialist cards lack comparison info1/5Medium
UI-09Break in flow between in-app map and directions1/5Medium
UI-12Pause Kit checkout does not confirm mode and total1/5Medium
UI-10Contact selection needs an unsignaled double-tap1/5Low
Flagged on the screens
Redesigned, before and after
UI-05High severityUI-01
Home: relief within reach

Relief used to live inside "Pain Mode", a label that itself confused users. A persistent "Get Relief" button now sits on every screen and opens SOS, Pause Space, supplies, a doctor and more. The insight card is marked "Predicted", and a "My Plan" card shows live progress.

UI-01Medium severity
Customize your plan: clear actions

Goal cards used an unlabeled icon that people could not read as add or remove. Each goal now has an explicit edit (pencil) and remove (×) control, and a progress header shows where you are in the 7 days.

UI-03UI-04Medium severity
Find a doctor: contrast and hierarchy

The dark hero header cropped its own headline and search bar, and dark-on-dark text was hard to read. The header is rebuilt at a fixed height, search sits on a white surface, and this task screen hides the tab bar.

UI-03Medium severity
Consult, book and confirm: closing the loop

Each task used to end at a dead-end "Done". The redesign adds a persistent "Your bookings" tracker on the Consult hub, so a booking stays visible after the fact.

05 · The takeaway

In high-stress wellness UX,
always design panic/relief actions
for 1-tap access.

When cognitive capacity drops, critical actions should become simpler, not harder to find.

1-TAP ACCESS
Reflection

What I learned from testing Pause.

Testing changed the product more than any single design decision did. These are the lessons I am carrying into my next project.

01

Put relief where the eye already is

Users never looked at the header, so the SOS and Relief icons placed there were invisible. Critical actions need to live in the user's path, not in a corner.Header: 0.00s of fixation in both concepts

02

Naming is part of the interface

"Pain Mode" itself confused people about where the Pause Kit lived. Plain, symptom-based words did more than any visual change.3 of 5 participants, UI-05

03

An average can hide rough edges

A SUS of 70.0 looked fine until I saw individual scores from 40.0 to 97.5. The spread showed me whom the design was still failing.SUS range 40.0 to 97.5

04

Small samples give direction, not proof

With 3 eye-tracking participants nothing reached significance. I learned to report that honestly and to decide on UX goals, not on one chart.All p > 0.05, n = 3

05

Accessibility is not final polish

Weak contrast and a cropped dark header changed what people could find at all. Contrast and hierarchy have to be designed in from the first screen.UI-03, UI-04

06

Close the loop after every task

Plans and bookings that disappear after confirmation make people doubt the system. Showing status after the fact builds trust.UI-01, UI-07

Next: re-test the redesigned flows with a larger group to check whether the fixes hold, starting with the persistent Get Relief button.
